correctness.rationale: The even-q vertex/crest locations and global rectangle inclusion are exact from the source definition. Any axis-centered radius is bounded by two vertical hyperbolic endpoints; the matching rectangle-contained disk attains the bound uniquely. It touches the boundary only at one smooth lower crest and one reflex upper corner. For a small horizontal shift, distance to the lower complete geodesic is arsinh(sinh(rho0)+t^2/(2Hy0)), and the nearest upper corner has cosh distance cosh(rho0)+t^2/(2ry0); the upper one-sided derivatives ensure the corner stays locally closest, and compactness excludes all other boundary contacts. Both grow strictly. An unrestricted maximizing disk must therefore be off the axis and reflected to a distinct maximum. Independent finite regression tests passed (100 even q); proof covers all even q.

value.rationale: The center of a largest inscribed ball is a natural size/shape invariant of the explicit nonconvex hyperbolic monotiles that have vanishing area and diameter. For convex reflection-symmetric bodies a maximizing center can always be chosen on the axis; this infinite even-parameter family demonstrates a strict, provable obstruction, with an exact sharp axis-constrained radius rather than only a computational counterexample. The nonconvex reflex cusp and smooth crest cause the failure. Neither global inradius nor an optimal quantitative gain is spuriously claimed.
